title: Your rule, rewritten
hook: rewrite your three-line rule from this block's start
tomorrow: two weeks left. where do you stand to look back?

segments.voice: Yesterday, appointed seasons, and a plan for when the calendar collides. Your year. Now all of it, in as few words as possible.
screen: `YOUR YEAR.` → `ALL OF IT, IN A FEW WORDS.`

segments.voice: People pin a quote above the desk, or write one line on the first page of a new notebook. A whole way of living, squeezed small enough to carry. The Talmud tells of a man who wanted to become Jewish and dared Hillel to teach him the whole Torah while he stood on one foot. Hillel didn't send him away.
screen: `ONE LINE ABOVE THE DESK.` → `THE WHOLE TORAH ON ONE FOOT.` → `HILLEL DIDN'T SEND HIM AWAY.`

segments.voice: Hillel's answer: what is hateful to you, do not do to your neighbor. That is the whole Torah; the rest is commentary. Go and learn. A neighbor tradition has a line close to it. Christians read in the Gospel of Matthew, in Jesus' words: "Therefore all things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets." What's shared is striking. Both put a whole body of teaching into how you treat another person, and both say this is the heart of the law. The honest differences are worth keeping. Hillel says what not to do; Matthew says what to do. And Hillel doesn't stop at the rule: he adds go and learn, so the one line opens into a lifetime of study. Each tradition reads its own line in its own way, and neither needs the other to be the same. At the start of this long stretch on living it, you wrote a rule of life in three lines. Now it gets rewritten, the way Hillel's one sentence asks: keep the heart, then keep learning. Something to tell a friend tonight: Hillel's whole-Torah sentence ends with homework, go and learn.
screen: `WHAT IS HATEFUL TO YOU, DON'T DO.` · `A NEIGHBOR: DO AS YOU'D BE DONE BY.` · `DON'T, AND DO: SHARED, AND DIFFERENT.` · `KEEP THE HEART. GO AND LEARN.` · then, large: `YOUR RULE OF LIFE.`

segments.voice: Take the three-line rule you wrote at the start of this stretch, or start fresh if you never wrote one. By hand, write it again: keep the line that held, change the one that didn't, and let one line be about how you treat other people.
screen: `YOUR THREE LINES.` · `KEEP WHAT HELD.` · `ONE LINE FOR OTHER PEOPLE.`

segments.voice: Your rule: a short rule of life, in your own words, kept at the heart and rewritten as you learn.
For the road: your rule of life, short enough to say on one foot. That's your own path, gathered up.

screen: `DAY 1777 COUNTS.` → `YOUR OWN PATH · 10 OF 10.` → `TOMORROW: TWO WEEKS LEFT. WHERE DO YOU STAND TO LOOK BACK?`

chat.meaning: Hillel and Matthew both put the heart of the law in how you treat others. Hillel's is 'don't do', Matthew's 'do', and Hillel adds 'go and learn'.
